title: Test types
intro: The kinds of automated test and where each sits in the test pyramid: unit, contract, integration and end-to-end, and the kinds beside it, each with an example for a Python application and for Terraform. The Languages tab lists the tools for the other main languages.
scope: Reference cards. Concepts are read from public articles and glossaries, tools from their own documentation. Code examples are fetched from those pages and shown unchanged. Free and open source tools only, and what ships with a language's own toolchain.

entries.name: The test pyramid
entries.summary: Many fast tests at the bottom, few slow ones at the top. The shape tells you how much testing to do at each layer.

version.name: Fowler: The Practical Test Pyramid
version.docs: martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html (26 February 2018). Tools: pytest 9.2.0, Pact Python 4.2.0, Testcontainers for Python 4.15.0, Playwright for Python 1.65.1, Terraform 1.17.2, Terratest 1.0.1

notes: The year of Mike Cohn's book is not stated on the pages read (unconfirmed).
The diagram uses four layers, as the rest of this topic does. Cohn's original has three: unit, service and user interface.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Mike Cohn's test pyramid has three layers: unit, service and user interface tests. The higher the layer, the slower and more fragile the test, so you write fewer of them.

items.alt: A pyramid in four layers. From the bottom: unit tests, integration tests, contract tests, end-to-end tests. The bottom layer is the widest and the top the narrowest.
items.caption: More tests at the bottom, fewer at the top.

items: Fowler says not to be too attached to the layer names: they are easy to misread. What matters is the idea of layers, with more of the cheap ones.

items.caption: What each layer is for. The last two columns are the examples in this topic.
rows: One function or class, on its own
That two sides agree on an interface
Your code with a database, a file system or a service
The whole running system, as a user would use it
Apply in a sandbox, then probe

sections.title: Start at the bottom
items: Write many small, fast unit tests. They tell you within seconds that a change broke something.
Add integration tests for the code that talks to things outside the application, such as a database.
Add contract tests where two services or teams meet, so each side can change without surprising the other.
Keep a few end-to-end tests for the most important paths. They give the most confidence but are slow and often flaky.
Push a test down to a lower layer when it can be checked there. Fowler: if a higher-level test finds an error and no lower-level test does, write a lower-level one.

sections.title: Do the same for Terraform
items: Terraform's own documentation uses the words too: a test that creates real infrastructure is described as analogous to an integration test, and a test run with command = plan as analogous to a unit test.
Fast checks come first: formatting, validation, a linter and a scanner. See [static analysis](#static-analysis).

sections.title: Common mistakes
items: The ice-cream cone: many slow high-level tests and few unit tests. Fowler warns it is a nightmare to maintain and takes way too long to run.
End-to-end tests that fail for no good reason. Fowler calls them notoriously flaky: browser quirks, timing issues, animations and pop-up dialogs.
Treating the layer names as law. People define unit, service and integration differently, so say what a test touches instead.
Mixing up acceptance tests with a layer. Fowler says they are orthogonal to the pyramid: you can write them at any layer.

sections.title: Other shapes
items: The pyramid is not the only shape. The testing trophy and the honeycomb put more weight on integration tests. See [Pyramid, trophy and honeycomb](#shapes).

sections.title: In one minute
items: A unit test calls a function or a class with chosen inputs and checks the result. It needs no database, network or deployed system, so it is fast and points at the code that broke.

rows: The logic of one function or class
That the real database or service behaves as you assume
A Terraform module's logic with command = plan
That the cloud accepts the resources

sections.title: What counts as a unit
items: Fowler: ask three people and you get four answers, and that is fine. In a functional language a unit is usually a function. In an object-oriented language it ranges from a method to a class.
Solitary tests replace every collaborator with a mock or stub. Sociable tests replace only the slow ones, such as code that calls a database or the network. See [Compare](#doubles).

sections.title: Python: pytest and unittest.mock
items: pytest finds functions named test_ and treats a plain assert as the check. pytest.raises checks that code raises an error.
unittest.mock, in the standard library, replaces a collaborator with a mock and checks how it was called.

items.title: Replace a method with a mock

sections.title: Terraform: terraform test with a plan
items: A run block in a .tftest.hcl file runs the module. With command = plan Terraform does not create new infrastructure, so the assertions check logic: names, counts, conditions. The documentation describes this as analogous to unit testing.
From Terraform 1.7.0 the data a provider returns can be mocked, so the test needs no cloud account.

sections.title: Habits and mistakes
items: Keep them fast. Fowler's advice is to write lots of small and fast unit tests.
Do not rely on mocks alone. They pass while the real parts do not fit together: that is what [integration tests](#integration) catch.

sections.title: In one minute
items: When one team builds a service and another calls it, the interface between them is a contract. A contract test checks that both sides keep to it.
In consumer-driven contract testing the consumer writes down what it needs. The provider runs those tests, and when they pass it knows it still serves its consumers (Fowler).

rows: The shape of requests and responses between two parties
That the provider's business logic is right
That a change on one side will not break the other
That the whole system works end to end
A module's inputs and outputs, in Terraform
That the resources it creates work

sections.title: Python: Pact
items: Pact is a tool for consumer-driven contracts. The consumer test runs against a Pact mock service and writes a pact file.
The provider test verifies the provider against the pact files and fails if a response no longer matches.
The Pact Python documentation also shows a Pact Broker, so pacts can be shared between teams without sharing a repository.

sections.title: Terraform: the module interface
items: A Terraform module's contract is its variables and outputs. A variable's validation block states what the module accepts.

items.title: A variable that rejects odd numbers

items: A test then checks both sides of the contract: a valid input is accepted and an invalid one fails. The expect_failures attribute lists the checkable objects that should fail.

items.title: A test that expects the validation to fail
This is a mapping
items.text: The Terraform documentation does not call this a contract test. It is the same idea applied to a module: its interface is tested without creating anything.

sections.title: Habits and mistakes
items: Use contract tests where teams meet. Fowler also uses them to keep the fakes in [integration tests](#integration) honest, by running contract tests against the fake and the real server.
A contract test says nothing about behaviour behind the interface. It does not replace the other layers.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Fowler: integration tests test the integration of your application with all the parts that live outside of it. To run them you need your own code and the component you integrate with.

rows: Real queries against a real database
The whole system through its user interface
That a client and a server really talk to each other
Logic that a unit test already covers
That Terraform really creates the resource
Whether users can use what was built

sections.title: Python: pytest with Testcontainers
items: Run the real dependency in a throwaway container for the length of the test. Testcontainers starts it, gives you the connection details and removes it afterwards.
The page shows it as a doctest. In a pytest suite the container is usually started in a fixture.

sections.title: Terraform: terraform test with an apply
items: By default each run block does a full apply, so the test creates real infrastructure and checks it. The documentation describes this as analogous to integration testing.
The example below chains three runs: one creates a bucket, one runs the configuration, one loads the result and counts it.

items.title: Real resources, real cost
items.text: Use a dedicated test account that can be purged. If a destroy fails, clean up by hand.

items: Terratest is the other common route: a Go test applies the configuration, checks the result and destroys it. Its code samples are loaded by script and cannot be fetched, so none is shown here: see its quick start.

sections.title: Habits and mistakes
items: Keep them to the code that touches the outside. They are slower than unit tests, so test the logic in unit tests.
Fowler: a fake of a dependency is only as good as its fidelity. [Contract tests](#contract) check it against the real one.

rows: run blocks with the default apply

sections.title: In one minute
items: End-to-end tests, also called broad stack tests, run against the completely integrated system. They give the biggest confidence that the software works (Fowler).
They are also notoriously flaky, so keep them to the few paths that must never break.

rows: A real user journey through every layer
Every edge case: lower layers do that
That the deployed parts are wired together
That a deployed Terraform configuration serves traffic

sections.title: Python: Playwright
items: Playwright drives a real browser. The pytest plugin gives each test a page, and expect checks what the page shows.
Point it at a deployed test environment, not at a mocked backend, or it is an integration test.

sections.title: Terraform: apply, then probe
items: An end-to-end test of infrastructure applies the whole root configuration in a sandbox and then checks that the result works, not only that resources exist.
A check block can run a data source after the apply and assert on it. Here it calls a health endpoint.
In a pipeline: apply in a throwaway environment, probe, then destroy. Terratest or a script can do the probing from outside Terraform.

sections.title: Habits and mistakes
items: Keep the number small. A wide top of the pyramid is the ice-cream cone.
When one fails, reproduce it at a lower layer and add a test there (Fowler's advice on where to put a test).

sections.title: What it is
items: ISTQB: analysis of software development artifacts, such as requirements or code, carried out without executing them, usually with a tool.
Python: mypy checks type annotations without running the program. A function without annotations is not checked.

Terraform: terraform fmt checks formatting, terraform validate checks syntax and consistency, a linter such as TFLint adds rules, and a scanner such as Checkov checks the configuration against policies.
Run these first in a pipeline: they need no cloud. Versions checked: mypy 2.4.1, Checkov 3.4.4, TFLint 0.66.0.

sections.title: What it is
items: ISTQB: a test suite that covers the main functionality of a component or system to determine whether it works properly before planned testing begins.
Python: a handful of end-to-end tests, such as the page loads and login works, run right after a deploy.
Terraform: after an apply, a check block that calls the service's health endpoint. See [end-to-end tests](#e2e).
A smoke test is defined by its purpose, not by a layer: it is a fast gate, usually made of a few tests from the layers above.

sections.title: What it is
items: ISTQB: testing of a previously tested program following a modification, to ensure that defects have not been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas as a result of the change. It is performed when the software or its environment is changed.
A regression suite is not a layer. It is the existing unit, integration and end-to-end tests, run again on each change.
Python: pytest run on each pull request. Terraform: terraform test run on each change to a module.

sections.title: What it is
items: Fowler: the higher you go in the pyramid, the more you test whether the features work correctly from a user's perspective. Treat the application as a black box: given a logged-in user and an article, when the user opens the article, then the article is shown.
He calls acceptance tests orthogonal to the pyramid: they can be written at any layer, and a lower layer is better when it is enough.
ISTQB defines acceptance testing as formal testing with respect to user needs, requirements and business processes, to decide whether to accept the system.
Python: a behaviour test in pytest, or a browser test with Playwright. Terraform: a test that asserts the outcome a requirement asks for.

links.label: Dodds: The Testing Trophy and Testing Classifications

notes: Spotify's article has no date on the page. The year is from its URL (unconfirmed).

sections.title: The three shapes
items: The pyramid puts most tests at the bottom, as unit tests. The trophy and the honeycomb put most of them in the middle, as integration tests.

Dodds says he never considered whether the trophy applied to microservices or backend services. He drew it for his own front-end code, and he says definitions of unit and integration differ from person to person.

Spotify says the pyramid can be harmful for microservices, because the complexity is in how services interact. Their honeycomb has mostly integration tests, a few implementation detail tests and ideally no integrated tests.
Fowler's warning about the ice-cream cone is the opposite mistake: too many tests at the top.

sections.title: What it is
items: ISTQB: coverage is the degree, expressed as a percentage, to which a specified coverage item has been exercised by a test suite. Code coverage determines which parts of the software the test suite executed and which it did not.
It is a measure of the tests, not a kind of test, so it sits beside the pyramid. It is usually collected while the [unit tests](#unit) run.

items.title: A number, not a proof
items.text: Fowler: test coverage is a useful tool for finding untested parts of a codebase. It is of little use as a numeric statement of how good your tests are.

coverage.py calls it the usual statement coverage

sections.title: How testing is organised
items: Tests are classes in `src/test/java`, the test source directory of the Maven standard layout. The build tool compiles and runs them: `mvn test` or `gradle test`.

Kotlin uses the same tools. The Kotlin documentation says tests written in Kotlin run together with existing Java tests in the same project, and that Kotlin/JVM supports JUnit 6. The `kotlin.test` library adds Kotlin's test utilities on top of JUnit.

rows: The test framework: annotations such as @Test, assertions, and the JUnit Platform that build tools launch
Mocking framework for unit tests in Java
Counts instructions, branches and lines. Has a Maven plug-in, and Gradle ships a plugin for it
Throwaway databases, browsers or anything else that runs in a Docker container, started from a JUnit test
Drives a browser natively, as a user would
Browser automation, same engine as the other Playwright languages

sections.title: Maven
items: Surefire runs the unit tests in the `test` phase. By default it picks the classes named `Test*.java`, `*Test.java` and `*Tests.java` (the page lists the full set).

Failsafe runs the integration tests in the `integration-test` phase and checks the result in `verify`, so the environment can be torn down in between. By default it picks `IT*.java`, `*IT.java` and `*ITCase.java`. Run it with `mvn verify`.

items.title: Failsafe bound to integration-test and verify

items: Coverage: the JaCoCo Maven plug-in. Its goals include `prepare-agent`, `report` and `check`. Versions checked: Surefire and Failsafe 3.6.1.

sections.title: Gradle
items: All JVM testing goes through one task type, `Test`. The `test` task runs JUnit, JUnit Platform or TestNG tests. `useJUnitPlatform()` selects the JUnit Platform.

source.label: Gradle: Testing in Java and JVM projects

items: Integration tests: the JVM Test Suite plugin (marked incubating) declares another suite, such as `integrationTest`, next to the built-in `test` suite.

Coverage: apply the `jacoco` plugin. With the Java plugin it adds a `jacocoTestReport` task, which writes an HTML report under `reports/jacoco/test/html` in the build directory. That task does not depend on `test`: run the tests first. Version checked: Gradle 9.9.1.

sections.title: How testing is organised
items: The tests are compiled into an executable. CTest, the test driver of CMake, runs the tests that a project registers with `enable_testing()` and `add_test()` and reports the results.
Coverage comes from the compiler: GCC with gcov, or Clang with llvm-cov.

rows: Mainly a unit testing framework for C++, with micro-benchmarks and simple BDD macros
Library for creating mock classes. Part of GoogleTest
Test coverage program of GCC. Compile with `--coverage` first
Perl scripts that turn the output of gcov or llvm-cov into reports
No C++ tool found for these layers. CTest runs whatever a project registers as a test

sections.title: How testing is organised
items: Unit tests sit in the same file as the code, in a module marked `#[cfg(test)]`, and can test private interfaces.
Integration tests are files in the `tests/` directory. They use the library as any other external code would, through its public interface only.
`cargo test` runs both, and the documentation tests (the `Doc-tests` part of its output).
